output:
*Interview with Mademoiselle Lina Ruedi, régleuse, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Mademoiselle, thank you for waiting. You know that Monsieur Monnier is dead. I am sorry to ask you to speak of it so soon. Tell me your place in the house.

MLLE RUEDI: I am the régleuse. I came up from Le Locle to learn the hairsprings, and he kept me because I was good at it. I work in the atelier on the top floor. I adjust the hairsprings and regulate what leaves the house. I was the best hand he had, though he would not say so at table.

MATTHEY: Tell me about the atelier.

MLLE RUEDI: His bench is under the long windows. The stove is at the back, and the precision regulator hangs on the wall where the light is best. Anything in this house that must be exact goes through that room.

MATTHEY: Let us come to the evening. Tell me about dinner.

MLLE RUEDI: When the temple struck nine, he made everyone show their watches, as he does every year. Mine was exact. The doctor's was two minutes ahead. Monsieur Girard would not take his out of his pocket.

MATTHEY: And after dinner?

MLLE RUEDI: I went up to the atelier to work beside him. The hall clock downstairs struck ten when the regulator showed twelve minutes to ten. He said what he always says about that clock. I will not repeat it, Inspector. It was an old joke between us. When the temple struck ten, the regulator agreed with the bell exactly.

MATTHEY: Did he send you away from the bench?

MLLE RUEDI: He did. He sent me downstairs when the regulator showed twenty past ten. The regulator was running then, and he was well. I went straight down to the kitchen.

MATTHEY: Had you seen him in the kitchen before that?

MLLE RUEDI: That afternoon I saw the master in the kitchen with Rosa's clock in his hands, laughing. I did not ask him why.

MATTHEY: Rosa's clock is the American alarm clock on the kitchen shelf?

MLLE RUEDI: Yes.

MATTHEY: Where were you when Madame began to play?

MLLE RUEDI: In the kitchen with Rosa. I looked at Rosa's clock when Madame's piano began. It showed two minutes to eleven. When the piano stopped, Rosa's clock showed eleven minutes past eleven.

MATTHEY: And after that?

MLLE RUEDI: I stayed in the kitchen with Rosa until after the temple struck eleven.

MATTHEY: Let me ask you about the repeater. Can you tell me how it speaks?

MLLE RUEDI: When you press the slide, it strikes the hours in low notes. Each quarter is a doubled note. The minutes past the quarter are high notes. So a listener hears the hour, then the quarter, then the minutes. It is a very fine sound, Inspector, and very hard to make.

MATTHEY: How long did he work on it?

MLLE RUEDI: Four years. He meant it for the new century. He would not let anyone else touch the striking work, and I did not ask him to.

MATTHEY: Did he speak to you about the repeater that evening?

MLLE RUEDI: He spoke about the work, as he always did. I will not guess at anything you have not asked me, Monsieur. I have told you what I saw and heard.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Mademoiselle. Please wait in the hall.
